references.text: The Preacher praises the joy of eating, drinking, and being glad—the same outlook expressed by the rich man: 'Eat, drink, and be merry!' ([ref:Fork 8:15|Ecclesiastes 8:15])

Isaiah describes the people's attitude in the face of judgment: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!'—a parallel to the rich man's thought of enjoying life without regard for God ([ref:Jes 22:13|Isaiah 22:13])

The Preacher reflects that there is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and let their soul enjoy what is good—a similar line of thinking to the rich man's self-satisfaction ([ref:Fork 2:24|Ecclesiastes 2:24])
The Preacher encourages the young to rejoice, but with a warning that God will judge—a contrast to the carefree attitude of the rich man ([ref:Fork 11:9|Ecclesiastes 11:9])

Paul quotes the mindset 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' as an example of an attitude without hope of resurrection—the same outlook held by the rich man ([ref:1 Kor 15:32|1 Corinthians 15:32])
James warns the rich who have stored up treasures for the last days and lived in luxury and pleasure—a direct parallel to the rich man's self-satisfied hoarding of goods ([ref:Jak 5:1-5|James 5:1-5])

Paul urges the rich not to set their hope on uncertain wealth—the rich man does exactly this by telling his soul that it has many good things stored up for many years ([ref:1 Tim 6:17|1 Timothy 6:17])

The immediately following verse shows God's response to the rich man's self-satisfaction: 'You fool! This very night your life will be demanded from you'—the judgment on his way of life ([ref:Luk 12:20|Luke 12:20])

Moses warns Israel not to forget the Lord when they have eaten their fill and live in good houses—the rich man's attitude is precisely the self-satisfaction warned against ([ref:5 Mos 6:10-12|Deuteronomy 6:10-12])
Hosea describes how the people became full and their hearts grew proud, and they forgot the Lord—a parallel to the rich man's materialism ([ref:Hos 13:6|Hosea 13:6])
